paras: The lynching of Lewis Edwards was the killing of a Black prisoner by masked men in the county jail at Jesup, Wayne County, Georgia, at about 3 a.m. on October 15, 1888. Edwards had been brought back from confinement to stand a new trial for the 1886 killing of a Jesup hotel proprietor when the men overpowered his guards and shot him in his cell. A coroner's jury attributed his death to an unknown unlawful mob, and the Atlanta Constitution's correspondent called it the first lynching on record in the county.

In January 1886 Robert J. Smith, proprietor of the Sunnyside house in Jesup, was shot and killed, and Lewis Edwards, a porter of the Commercial house, was charged with the killing. At the March 1887 term of Wayne superior court a jury convicted him of murder with a recommendation of mercy, and Judge Atkinson sentenced him to life imprisonment.

His counsel, E. D. Graham and S. W. Hitch, won a motion for a new trial. On October 12, 1888, Gov. Gordon ordered the penitentiary keeper to deliver Edwards to the Wayne County sheriff to be held until the new trial was decided.

On Sunday, October 14, Sheriff J. D. Robinson brought Edwards from Greston, where he had been held since March 1887, arriving at Jesup on the 11:15 train. Because the jail was insecure, the sheriff placed a guard of four men around it, buried the jail keys near a pine sapling so the guards could not be made to give them up, and went to bed at the Jesup house.

At about 3 o'clock a party of men disguised with oil cloth and rags rushed the guards at their fire outside the jail yard, held them at pistol point and took their guns. The guards Thomas Reddish and T. J. Lundy put the party at six to twelve men, about three of whom entered the jail.
The men who entered the cell fired twelve balls into Edwards's head and body, killing him instantly, and the party left without saying anything more.

The coroner's jury, after hearing the four guards and the sheriff, found that Edwards died on October 15, 1888, of leaden balls shot into his body "by an unlawful mob, with malice aforethought," its members unknown. No report of arrests, grand jury action or charges appears in the coverage.

The story reached the national press through a dispatch dated Jessup, October 16, which ran that day in the Alexandria Gazette and the San Antonio Daily Light and on October 17 in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Indianapolis Journal and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette. The wire stated flatly that Smith "was murdered by Lewis Edwards, colored," although the conviction had been set aside, and headlines ranged from "Murderer Shot" and "A Negro Murderer Shot" to "Shot Without Trial." Condensed versions ran in news-summary columns into late October, from New Hampshire and Maryland to Tennessee and Louisiana.

The Savannah Morning News called Edwards "the black murderer of R. J. Smith," and the Atlanta Constitution headed its special "The First Lynching," writing that the case "was tried before Judge Lynch this morning." A Michigan weekly that condensed the special opened with "Masked men wreaked vengeance upon a murderer."

The one sharp dissent came in an Atlanta letter printed by the Republican Indianapolis Journal on October 18 under the headline "How Colored Men Are Treated in the Empire State of the South." Its writer called the killing a "cruel lynching" by "a mob of white Democrats" and "wholly indefensible," and folded it into a campaign-season indictment of Georgia Democrats alongside a destroyed jury list and a counted-out Black legislator.

The Indianapolis Journal's correspondent claimed that Edwards had killed the landlord "Under great provocation and in self-defense" and that the mob struck because the new trial would have acquitted him, a version no other report carries. Other details vary: the Jesup Sentinel and the coroner's verdict spell the name Louis, the Richmond Times dates Smith's death to 1883 rather than 1886, and condensed items place the shooting on "Sunday night" rather than early Monday.

reader.title: Lynching of Lewis Edwards
bases: A party of masked men overpowered the jail guard at Jesup, took the keys and shot the prisoner Lewis Edwards dead in his cell (A4, A16, A17).

Edwards was shot dead in jail by masked men whom the guards numbered at six to twelve, and the coroner's jury called them 'an unlawful mob' (A16); he was awaiting a new trial for the killing of R. J. Smith, and the local special called it a case 'tried before Judge Lynch' (A17).

The wire report (A2, A5), the Savannah Morning News dispatch (A4), the Atlanta Constitution special (A17) and the Jesup Sentinel's account of the inquest (A16) agree that masked men shot Edwards in the Jesup jail about 3 a.m. on October 15, 1888.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A dispatch dated Jessup, October 16, said Smith had been 'murdered' by Edwards in January 1886, that Edwards had won a new trial, and that masked men entered the jail at 3 o'clock Monday morning and shot him dead.

accounts.label: Guards and sheriff before the coroner's jury
accounts.gist: The guards said masked, armed men surprised them by their fire, disarmed them, found the buried keys and sent about three men into the jail; the sheriff said he had hidden the keys and gone to bed at the Jesup house.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Edwards died on October 15, 1888, of leaden balls shot into his body by an unlawful mob unknown to the jury.

accounts.label: Atlanta Republican correspondent
accounts.gist: Edwards had killed the landlord 'Under great provocation and in self-defense'; a white mob of Democrats killed him because the new trial would have acquitted him.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under heads such as 'Murderer Shot', 'Shot Dead by Masked Men' and 'Shot Without Trial', stating as fact that Smith 'was murdered by Lewis Edwards'.
The Georgia papers called Edwards 'the black murderer' and treated the killing as a local first, 'tried before Judge Lynch', without comment on the mob.
The True Northerner wrote that 'Masked men wreaked vengeance upon a murderer'; the Richmond Times headed it 'A Negro Murderer Shot'.
The Indianapolis Journal's Atlanta letter, headed 'How Colored Men Are Treated in the Empire State of the South', called the lynching 'wholly indefensible' and used it against Georgia Democrats.

conflicts.note: The coroner's verdict and the local dispatch give October 15; 'Sunday night' in condensed items refers to the night that ended in the 3 a.m. shooting.
The Jesup Sentinel and the coroner's verdict use Louis; most wire copies and the Atlanta special use Lewis.
1883 appears only in the Richmond Times copy of the wire, against the local special and the 1887 trial date.
Robinson is the name in the sworn inquest testimony.
